notes.meaning: God kept His promise to Sarah by visiting her with His power and grace. After twenty-five years of waiting, the Lord showed that His word never fails. He always acts at the exact moment He chooses.

Sarah became pregnant and gave birth to a son for Abraham in his extreme old age. This took place at the very time God had set beforehand. The birth was a miracle of divine power when both parents were past the age of having children.
Abraham named his newborn son Isaac, exactly as God had told him to do. The name means laughter. It turned the couple's earlier doubt into true joy and praise.

Abraham circumcised Isaac when the boy was eight days old, following God's command. Circumcision was a physical cutting that served as the sign of God's covenant, His special agreement with Abraham's family. Isaac was the first child in Scripture to receive this sign on the eighth day.

Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born. This was twenty-five years after God first promised to make him a great nation. His advanced age highlighted that Isaac was entirely a gift from God.

Sarah rejoiced that God had given her a reason to laugh with pure happiness. She knew that everyone who heard this amazing news would celebrate with her. God turned her past doubt into shared delight.
Sarah marvelled that an elderly woman like her was nursing a baby for Abraham. No one would have believed such a thing could happen by natural strength. Her wonder gave all the glory to God alone.

Isaac grew and was weaned from his mother's milk, which usually happened around age three. Abraham threw a large feast to mark this important step in the young boy's life. The celebration publicly honoured Isaac as the child who would carry on the family blessing.

Sarah noticed Ishmael, who was about seventeen years old, mocking young Isaac during the celebration. Ishmael played on the meaning of Isaac's name in a disrespectful way. Sarah saw this scorn as a threat to Isaac's place as the true heir.

differ.view: Ishmael's mocking was likely light teasing or ridicule about Sarah's old age rather than deep malice.
Ishmael's actions showed bitter contempt and were an early persecution of the spiritual seed of promise.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew verb can mean playing, suggesting Sarah may have reacted out of jealousy at seeing the two boys together rather than from open hostility.

notes.meaning: Sarah demanded that Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away so that the slave boy would not share the inheritance with Isaac. She wanted to protect Isaac's unique role as the sole child of promise. This separation showed that God's covenant blessing would pass through Isaac alone.

differ.view: Sarah casting out Hagar pictures how human effort under the law cannot share an inheritance with righteousness received through faith.
Hagar represents the covenant of works, showing that those relying on human effort are cast out from the covenant of grace.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Hagar is seen as a type of the earthly Jerusalem and the old synagogue, while Sarah represents the church of the Gentiles.

notes.meaning: Sarah's demand deeply troubled Abraham because Ishmael was his own son whom he loved. He did not want to treat the boy harshly or cast him out into hardship. Abraham struggled between his natural fatherly love and the conflict inside his home.

God spoke to Abraham and told him not to be distressed over the boy or Hagar. The Lord told him to listen to Sarah, because Abraham's promised line would be counted through Isaac. God's covenant plan had to go forward even when it was painful for human feelings.

God comforted Abraham by promising to make Ishmael into a great nation as well. Ishmael received this blessing because he was Abraham's son. Even though he was not the heir of the covenant, God still cared for his future.

Abraham got up early the next morning, gave Hagar bread and a skin of water, and sent her away with Ishmael. She wandered without a clear destination in the dry wilderness of Beersheba. Abraham obeyed God promptly, trusting the Lord to protect his son.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Abraham gave Hagar minimal supplies, reflecting how the low legal standing of an enslaved woman left her vulnerable in the ancient world.

notes.meaning: The water in the leather skin ran out under the desert sun, leaving Ishmael faint and exhausted. Hagar placed the young man under the shade of a desert bush to shield him from the heat. She had reached the end of all her strength and supplies.

Hagar moved about a bowshot away because she could not bear to watch her son die. She sat down in the sand and wept aloud in deep anguish. In her complete helplessness, she gave up all hope for survival.

God heard the cries of the suffering boy from where he lay on the ground. An angel called to Hagar from heaven, telling her not to fear because God had paid attention to Ishmael's voice. Even in a desolate wasteland, God hears the cries of those in trouble.

The angel commanded Hagar to get up, lift the boy, and hold him firmly by the hand. God reaffirmed His promise that Ishmael would live and grow into a great nation. This promise gave Hagar renewed courage to care for her child.

God opened Hagar's eyes so she could see a well of fresh water nearby. She filled her water container and gave her dying son a drink, saving his life. God provided what they needed most right when all human hope was gone.

God stayed with Ishmael as he grew into manhood in the wilderness. He learned how to survive in the wild and became skilled with the bow and arrow. God's watchful care protected him in earthly matters just as He had said.

Ishmael settled in the dry wilderness of Paran in the desert region. His mother arranged a marriage for him with a woman from her homeland of Egypt. This established Ishmael's family line outside the borders of Canaan.

King Abimelech and his army commander Phicol visited Abraham. They saw clearly that God was blessing Abraham and prospering him in everything he did. The local ruler wanted to maintain peace with a neighbor who had God's favor.

Abimelech asked Abraham to swear a solemn oath before God not to deal falsely with him or his descendants. The king asked Abraham to show the same kindness that Gerar had shown to him while he lived there as a guest. He wanted a firm peace treaty between their households.

Abraham agreed to the proposal and promised by oath to deal fairly with Abimelech. Taking an honest oath to make peace was a lawful and godly act. Abraham showed himself ready to be an honorable neighbor in the land.

Before completing the agreement, Abraham brought a complaint about a water well that Abimelech's servants had seized. Water was rare and precious in that dry climate, making wells vital for survival. Abraham wanted to settle this dispute openly before entering into a formal covenant.

Abimelech replied that he had no idea who had seized the well and had never heard about it until that very day. He had not authorized the wrongdoing and was ready to resolve the issue. Honest communication helped both leaders clear up the misunderstanding.

Abraham gave sheep and cattle to Abimelech as gifts of friendship, and the two men made a covenant together. In this ancient custom, sharing animals and making vows bound both parties to keep their word. This pact created a lasting bond of peace between them.
Abraham separated seven young female lambs from the rest of the flock. He placed them by themselves for a specific purpose in the ceremony. This deliberate act caught the attention of the king.

Abimelech asked Abraham why he had set those seven lambs apart from the others. He understood the general covenant gifts, but he did not know the meaning of this special group. Abraham used the king's question to resolve the dispute about the well.

Abraham explained that Abimelech's acceptance of the seven lambs would serve as proof that Abraham had dug the well. Taking the lambs acted as a public receipt confirming Abraham's ownership. This wise step prevented any future quarrels over water rights.

The site was named Beersheba, which means well of the oath or well of the seven. The name marked the solemn vows both men made to each other by the well. It stood as a permanent reminder of their peaceful pact.

After completing their treaty at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol returned home to the land of the Philistines. The agreement gave Abraham security to live without fear of conflict. God granted His servant a season of quiet and safety among the local people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Philistines mentioned here were early Semitic inhabitants of the region, distinct from the sea-faring Philistines who arrived from the Aegean around 1200 BC.

notes.meaning: Abraham planted a leafy tamarisk tree in Beersheba and worshipped the Lord, the Eternal God. Planting a slow-growing tree that needs deep water showed Abraham's trust that God would provide long-term peace in the land. He openly thanked the everlasting God for His continuing care.

Abraham lived in the Philistine country as a peaceful guest for a long time. Even though he enjoyed safety under the treaty, he remained a pilgrim waiting for God's full promise to be completed. His long stay there testified to God's steady faithfulness in his life.
